evidence.title: Political DEBATE: Efficient Zero-shot and Few-shot Classifiers for Political Text
evidence.claim: Political DEBATE base and large are DeBERTa V3 NLI models (starting from Laurer et al. 2023 NLI checkpoints) further trained on PolNLI, 201,691 documents and 852 hypotheses. Each document is paired with a templated hypothesis and labeled entail or not entail. Full-training base hyperparameters: learning rate 2e-5 for 20 epochs (Appendix C.1). Few-shot runs used the default learning rate for 5 epochs with no tuning.
evidence.system_side: finetune_debate.py starts from mlburnham/Political_DEBATE_base_v1.0 and builds three premise-hypothesis pairs per release using the template 'This text is {}.' with the labels supportive of, opposed to or critical of, and neutral toward or not about credit unions. The true label gets entailment and the other two get contradiction. Script defaults: learning rate 2e-5, 3 epochs, batch 8.
evidence.transfer: Direct provenance: same released checkpoint and same NLI framing. Epoch count differs: 3 in the script, 5 in the paper's few-shot runs, 20 in the paper's full training. Whether 3 epochs at lr 2e-5 suits a 552-row fine-tune is untested against the CU gold.

evidence.title: Political DEBATE: Efficient Zero-shot and Few-shot Classifiers for Political Text
evidence.claim: The paper recommends the large model for zero-shot and most few-shot use, and the base model for simple few-shot or supervised work. On COVID threat minimization the base model largely fails zero-shot and does not match the supervised Electra classifier (MCC 0.66) in accuracy at 100 samples; the text gives no base MCC. The large model matches the classifier at 10 samples (MCC 0.67, accuracy 87 percent) and exceeds it at 25 (MCC 0.69, accuracy 88 percent). On Polistance quote tweets, Claude 3.5 scored MCC 0.29, base 0.62 and large 0.88.
evidence.system_side: Training and inference default to the base checkpoint (finetune_debate.py:32; stage5_debate.py:38). The brain actor note records that base was chosen because the machine is CPU-only, a large fine-tune takes about 3 hours with memory risk, and the plan originally named large. Zero-shot base reached 53 percent accuracy with oppose F1 0.08 on the 156-row Claude-labeled test. Fine-tuned base scored 0.796 on the 760-row gold frame and 0.571 on the adversarial frame.
evidence.transfer: Applies only if CU stance with sign-flip targets counts as bespoke in the paper's sense, which the oppose F1 of 0.08 suggests but does not prove. The paper reports MCC on binary tasks; the system task is 3-class. The base-versus-large gap on the adversarial frame has not been measured.

evidence.title: Political DEBATE: Efficient Zero-shot and Few-shot Classifiers for Political Text
evidence.claim: The paper recommends short, simple hypotheses close to the training templates, and says tasks needing long or multi-condition hypotheses call for few-shot training. During training, neutral and contradiction were merged into not-entail (footnote on p.6), so neutral is not a trained positive concept.
evidence.system_side: The neutral hypothesis is the compound 'neutral toward or not about credit unions'. Inference scores the three hypotheses independently (multi_label=True) and takes the argmax, after truncating documents to 3000 characters. Training uses a 1600-character lede within a 384-token window.
evidence.transfer: Fine-tuning on 552 rows partly offsets the template mismatch. Whether splitting neutral into a not-about-CUs hypothesis plus an explicit neutral rule beats the compound hypothesis is untested. Press releases are longer than the paper's short-document zero-shot condition.

evidence.title: Political DEBATE: Efficient Zero-shot and Few-shot Classifiers for Political Text
evidence.claim: The paper uses MCC as its primary metric, chosen for its relative robustness compared with F1 and accuracy on binary classification (p.9). It excludes GPT-4o from the benchmark because GPT-4o was used in label validation, and it discourages benchmarking OpenAI models on PolNLI for that reason (p.9-10). The paper does not say this exclusion would inflate agreement.
evidence.system_side: The 87.2 percent accuracy, macro-F1 0.833 and kappa 0.771 are agreement with the Claude reference on the 156-row held-out test (brain actor note, 2026-06-22). Separately, live fine-tuned accuracy 0.839 with kappa 0.760 on n=87 held-out (2026-06-30). The topic note reports about 85 percent and kappa 0.76 on a member-grouped human gold. No MCC is recorded.
evidence.transfer: Agreement with the LLM that generated the labels is not accuracy against humans. Quote only human-gold figures and name the denominator (156, 87 or 760 rows). Do not merge the 156-row 87.2 percent figure, the n=87 0.839 figure and the about 85 percent member-grouped figure.

evidence.title: Political DEBATE: Efficient Zero-shot and Few-shot Classifiers for Political Text
evidence.claim: The paper says NLI classifiers work best zero-shot on commonly understood concepts such as support for a person or policy. They are weaker on bespoke concepts needing specialized domain knowledge, where few-shot or supervised training is advised. This is qualitative guidance; the paper does not test a decomposition.
evidence.system_side: CU alignment is scored as a stance hop and a valence hop. The concept note reports stance 0.915 and valence 0.689 on the 400 tweet golds, measured 2026-07-04, with valence as the bottleneck. The valence registry was derived from the user's own valence judgments (11 entries; 5-fold CV compose 0.782). A hand-curated 14-entry seed exists but the curated path is an unbuilt option. Zero-shot DEBATE misses implicit policy-anti stances.
evidence.transfer: The concept note does not name DEBATE as the 0.915 stance-hop model; it refers to the stance stack. The paper supports the pattern, not the mechanism. Valence is a bespoke concept, which is the paper's stated condition for weakness.

evidence.title: Political DEBATE: Efficient Zero-shot and Few-shot Classifiers for Political Text
evidence.claim: NLI zero-shot works best when labels can be derived from the text alone, without meta-knowledge about who wrote it (p.16). On quote tweets, which carry two opinions from two people, the hardest set: Claude 0.29, base 0.62, large 0.88 MCC. DeBERTa Large NLI had negative correlation with the correct labels on that set.
evidence.system_side: The planned Phase 2 branches the NLI hypothesis by speaker_source so ACU-authored rows get 'advocacy group praising or criticizing this member', then retrains. The plan is blocked on ACU-signal labels, and its gate is held-out accuracy of at least 0.851.
evidence.transfer: The meta-knowledge condition applies directly, since the paper names authorship. ACU texts about a member resemble two-voice quote tweets only by analogy; the paper gives no result for advocacy-group-about-member texts. Base-versus-large on such texts is untested.

evidence.title: Political DEBATE: Efficient Zero-shot and Few-shot Classifiers for Political Text
evidence.claim: On the COVID threat-minimization task only, the large model matches a supervised classifier at 10 samples (MCC 0.67 vs 0.66) and exceeds it at 25 (MCC 0.69). The base model, per the text, fails to match the supervised classifier's accuracy at 100 samples. The claim is confined to that bespoke task.
evidence.system_side: build_media_blend.py code comment: DEBATE alone scores 0.796 on the 760-row gold frame and 0.571 on the adversarial frame, against 0.837 and 0.765 for the stacked meta-reader. The vault system note reports a LinearSVC at 83.9 percent on n=87 and gives 0.757 for a transformer, which is not located in code. Fine-tuned DEBATE accuracy of 0.839 on the same n=87 ties the SVM.
evidence.transfer: The paper's claim concerns the large model, not the base. A fine-tuned base losing to a stack on a bespoke CU target is consistent with the paper. The SVM-versus-transformer pair is not a DEBATE result and 0.757 is unverified. The 760-row stack is a meta-learner, not a supervised classifier alone.

evidence.title: Positioning Political Texts with Large Language Models by Asking and Averaging
evidence.claim: Asking an LLM directly for a 0-100 position score (JSON only, temperature 0, NA allowed) gives text-level positions. GPT-4o r=0.92 against crowd means, but on the 557 of 899 tweets that received a score (NA excluded). API cost about 1.5 USD for 900 tweets versus 1,626 GBP for human coding. Table A2 ENO for the LLMs in the table is 3 to 7 human raters.
evidence.system_side: claude_stance.py is a Claude API rater that returns JSON only (stance, confidence, reason). Its docstring says it pre-labels the ~400 hand-coding set and is the third ensemble member beside fine-tuned DEBATE and the bill signal. Code matches this description.
evidence.transfer: The paper tests GPT-4, GPT-4o, MiXtral and Llama 3 (Table 1 lists no Claude model) on left-right and subsidy dimensions against independent crowd and expert benchmarks. The system rater is categorical (support/oppose/neutral), not a 0-100 scale, and its gold labels were pre-labelled by the same rater. The paper's accuracy figures cannot be quoted as properties of the Claude rater.

evidence.title: Positioning Political Texts with Large Language Models by Asking and Averaging
evidence.claim: LLM direct query beats text classifiers on the paper's own benchmarks. Tweets: GPT-4o r=0.92 versus fine-tuned BERT 0.78, tf-idf 0.66, GloVe 0.63. Senators: GPT-4o 0.97 versus BERT 0.93, tf-idf 0.90. The paper says no classifier matches the best LLMs on within-party differences. Its classifiers are typicality readers (naive Bayes tf-idf, BERT, GloVe) trained on about 1 million party-labelled Congress tweets, not stance classifiers trained on human stance labels. No linear SVM is tested.
evidence.system_side: fec/stance/train_tweet_stance.py builds a LinearSVC on word and char_wb TF-IDF with a CV grid over C, so the system's best classical reader is the SVM as described. The 83.9% accuracy, macro-F1 0.816 (n=87), 0.757 transformer and 0.737 CV (399 golds) figures are not in the code and were not checked against outputs.
evidence.transfer: The paper compares continuous left-right positions, scored by correlation, against party-typicality readers. The system compares three-class target stance, scored by accuracy, against a stance-trained SVM. The paper does not test a stance-trained linear model, so it cannot contradict the system's SVM-over-transformer result. Treat it as a head-to-head test to run.

evidence.title: Positioning Political Texts with Large Language Models by Asking and Averaging
evidence.claim: Sec 2.1: a document's position is the average of the sentence or tweet scores for which the LLM returned a numeric score, so NA units are dropped from the average. App E, Table A1 (GPT-4o row): tweets that received a score had 18.7 human ratings on average versus 11.6 for unscored tweets, which the paper reads as NA marking low political content.
evidence.system_side: SIGN maps neutral to 0.0 and build_media_blend adds sign times intensity times decay divided by len(hits) per post, so neutral posts contribute zero and are not removed from any count. claude_stance.py sets stance to neutral with confidence 0.0 when the API call fails or the reply cannot be parsed, so API failure and real neutrality look the same in the output.
evidence.transfer: The paper validates averaging for left-right placement, not for CU advocacy intensity. Averaging measures position while the blend sums volume. Whether volume should count is Paul's policy call, not a recommendation to normalise. Any change needs Paul's ruling and zero-rank-delta or look discipline.

evidence.title: Positioning Political Texts with Large Language Models by Asking and Averaging
evidence.claim: Sec 3.4 and Fig 5 (36 coal-subsidy speeches, 10 languages, six-language crowd mean): GPT-4o overall r=0.93, with Against 0.91 and For 0.80. Against-group r is 0.07 for GPT-4 Turbo, 0.04 for MiXtral 8X22B and 0.05 for Llama 3 70B, but GPT-4o is strong within Against. Tweets within party for GPT-4o: 0.68 Democrats and 0.66 Republicans (Fig 1).
evidence.system_side: apply_two_hop_stance.py docstring states a model stance hop of 0.915 and a model valence hop of 0.689 on the 400 tweet golds, with a composed ceiling of 0.872. The curated-registry accuracy of 0.782 and the bottleneck reading are not in the file and were not checked against outputs.
evidence.transfer: The paper tests one policy dimension (coal subsidy, 36 speeches) against crowd benchmarks. The weak within-Against cases belong to models other than GPT-4o, which is strong in both groups. The paper does not discuss within-camp weakness, so any link to the valence hop is the analyst's inference and suggestive only.

evidence.title: Playing to the Gallery: Emotive Rhetoric in Parliaments
evidence.claim: Emotiveness is measured valence-agnostically: percent emotive words (ANEW, 851 emotive seeds) minus percent neutral words (970 neutral seeds). Skip-gram embeddings expand the dictionary to 2,015 emotive and 2,095 neutral UK words, following Rice and Zorn (2019). Scale runs from -100 to +100; mean 0.88, SD 8.95.
evidence.system_side: Live press intensity is abs(lsd_net_norm), i.e. abs(pos - neg)/words, chosen by the CU_S5_INTENSITY default of net_norm. stage5_lsd.R also emits lsd_charge = (pos + neg)/words, used only when INTENSITY is charge. The LSD tone dictionary is generic with no domain expansion (not re-verified in this pass).
evidence.transfer: Applies if 'how heated' should mean emotional charge regardless of direction. The paper validates on parliamentary speech, not press releases. Switching intensity changes press_value and the Press pillar, a change-control decision for Paul, not a recommendation here.

evidence.title: Measuring Emotion in Parliamentary Debates with Automated Textual Analysis
evidence.claim: Domain lexicon from 200 emotion seeds (100 positive, 100 negative lemmas) using GloVe vectors of 300 dimensions per lemma-PoS pair, symmetric window 15, 108,506 lemma types at frequency 10 or more. Each lemma score is its summed cosine to positive seeds minus summed cosine to negative seeds, scaled to [-1,1]. The top and bottom 2,000 are kept (4,200 words). Table 1 lists compound (verb) at -1.00.
evidence.system_side: Opt-in offline expand_tone_lexicon helper trains GloVe on the scraped CU press corpus and writes a CSV of cosine-nearest candidates to 10 positive and 10 negative seeds for analyst promotion. Live scoring stays on the curated TONE_LEXICON, per the helper's own comment.
evidence.transfer: Parallel method, not the source: the helper header cites Rice and Zorn 2018 for the seed-to-vocabulary logic. Its GloVe settings differ from Rheault's (rank 50, skip-gram window 5, minimum count 5, at least 50 documents). Its seeds mix stance words (support, champion, protect) with affect words. The press corpus is far smaller than Hansard, so vectors will be noisier. Rheault's own odd top entries show the risk. The analyst review step is the safeguard; the top and bottom cut has no in-domain validation.

evidence.title: Measuring Emotion in Parliamentary Debates with Automated Textual Analysis
evidence.claim: The long-run trend reproduces with NRC, OpinionFinder and SentiWordNet (S1 Fig, text description only; figure not extracted). Polarity is a signed weighted sum over all lemmas. Film-review validation reaches up to 80 percent accuracy; no parliamentary validation is reported in the extracted text. Recession -0.198 (SE 0.062) and election +0.187 (SE 0.069) shift the annual polarity change, pooled over government and opposition, N=104 years, Table 2 Model 1 (UNSTRATIFIED). The yearly polarity series has a unit root.
evidence.system_side: LSD2015 is applied unchanged to congressional press releases. lsd_tone returns net/words and (pos+neg)/words. run_stage5 defaults INTENSITY to net_norm, so heat is abs(net/words), multiplied by the stance sign to form press_value.
evidence.transfer: Rheault measures direction; Paul uses tone only as an intensity multiplier. Under net_norm a release dense in both positive and negative words scores near zero heat, so the paper gives no support for reading abs(polarity) as intensity. The lsd_charge option is closer to an intensity construct. Period effects matter only if members' release windows differ in date coverage. Westminster debate text is not US press-release text.
